# Maternal complications during pregnancy

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Obstetrics/gynecology > Pregnancy and prenatal care > Maternal complications during pregnancy*

[Original Article Link](/library/_q05ah)

---

## Summary

Maternal complications during <u>pregnancy</u> include metabolic conditions, hemorrhage, infectious diseases, and dermatologic conditions. <u>Hyperemesis gravidarum</u> is a severe form of <u>nausea and vomiting</u> in <u>pregnancy</u> characterized by <u>ketonuria</u> and weight loss and typically requires inpatient admission, IV fluid hydration, and <u>antiemetic therapy</u>. <u>Cervical insufficiency</u> refers to the inability of the <u>cervix</u> to retain a <u>pregnancy</u> in the <u>second trimester</u> in the absence of <u>labor</u>, contractions, or other pathologies; <u>cervical cerclage</u> may be required. <u>Pregnancy dermatoses</u> are pruritic conditions that occur during <u>pregnancy</u> or in the immediate <u>postpartum period</u> and include <u>gestational pemphigoid</u> and <u>polymorphic eruption of pregnancy</u>. Other maternal <u>complications of pregnancy</u> include <u>hypertensive pregnancy disorders</u>, <u>pregnancy-associated liver diseases</u>, and <u>gestational diabetes</u>.




See also “<u>Common discomforts during pregnancy</u>.”

---

## Overview

### Metabolic complications




* <u>Hypertensive pregnancy disorders</u>

* <u>Gestational hypertension</u>

* <u>Preeclampsia</u>

* <u>Eclampsia</u>

* <u>Gestational diabetes</u>

* <u>Pregnancy-associated liver diseases</u>

* <u>Hyperemesis gravidarum</u>

* <u>HELLP syndrome</u>

* <u>AFLP</u>

* <u>Cholestasis of pregnancy</u>





### Hemorrhagic complications




* <u>First trimester</u>: See “<u>Vaginal bleeding</u>.”

* <u>Spontaneous abortion</u>

* <u>Ectopic pregnancy</u>

* Second and <u>third trimester</u>: See “<u>Antepartum hemorrhage</u>.”

* <u>Placenta previa</u>

* <u>Abruptio placentae</u>

* <u>Uterine rupture</u>

* Other: <u>Fetomaternal hemorrhage</u>





### Infectious complications




* <u>Chorioamnionitis</u>

* <u>UTI in pregnancy</u>

* <u>Sexually transmitted infections</u> (e.g., <u>pelvic inflammatory disease in pregnancy</u>)





### Other complications




* <u>Pregnancy dermatoses</u>

* <u>Pregnancy luteoma</u>

## Hyperemesis gravidarum

* Definition: severe, persistent <u>nausea and vomiting</u> associated with a > 5% loss of prepregnancy weight and <u>ketonuria</u> with no other identifiable cause [[2]](/library/yqYdaq)

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* <u>Multiple gestation</u>

* <u>Hydatidiform mole</u>

* <u>Nulliparity</u>

* <u>Migraine headaches</u>

* <u>GERD</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>

* Physical signs of <u>dehydration</u>

* <u>Hypersalivation</u>,

* <u>Orthostatic hypotension</u>

* <u>Malnourishment</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u>

* <u>Laboratory analysis</u>

* <u>Electrolyte</u> disturbances: <u>hypokalemia</u> and <u>hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis</u> or <u>metabolic acidosis</u>  [[3]](/library/AhcRgX0)

* Signs of <u>dehydration</u> (e.g., ↑ <u>hematocrit</u>)

* <u>Ketonuria</u>

* Treatment

* <u>Antiemetic therapy</u>: See “<u>Antiemetic therapy for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy</u>.” [[2]](/library/yqYdaq)
* May require <u>glucocorticoid</u> therapy (see stepwise approach above)

* <u>IV fluid resuscitation</u>/replacement (see <u>IV fluid therapy</u>)

* <u>Electrolyte</u> and <u>thiamine</u> repletion DOSAGE

* <u>Enteral feeding</u> or <u>TPN</u> is recommended in patients with persistent symptoms and weight loss despite <u>antiemetic therapy</u>. [[2]](/library/yqYdaq)

* Complications  [[4]](/library/ldcvJY0)[[5]](/library/Ndc-JY0)

* Maternal

* <u>Hypokalemia</u>

* <u>Wernicke encephalopathy</u>

* Fetal

* <u>Intrauterine growth restriction</u>

* <u>Low birth weight</u>

* <u>Preterm birth</u>

* Acute management checklist for hyperemesis gravidarum [[2]](/library/yqYdaq)[[6]](/library/BqYz0q)[[7]](/library/qqYCzJ)[[8]](/library/LiYwHK) 

* Rule out alternate etiologies (see <u>differential diagnosis of nausea and vomiting</u>).

* Identify and treat <u>dehydration</u> (see <u>IV fluids</u>).

* <u>Thiamine</u> repletion

* <u>Electrolyte repletion</u>

* IV <u>antiemetic therapy</u> (see <u>antiemetic therapy for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy</u>)

* Consider <u>enteral tube</u> feeding (nasogastric/nasoduodenal) or <u>TPN</u>.

* Closely monitor <u>vitals</u> and urine output.

* Monitor urine <u>ketones</u>, <u>BMP</u>, and body weight daily.

* Inpatient admission

* Consult <u>OB/GYN</u>.

## Cervical insufficiency

### Definition




<u>Cervical insufficiency</u> is the inability of the <u>cervix</u> to retain a <u>pregnancy</u> in the <u>second trimester</u> in the absence of contractions, <u>labor</u>, or other underlying pathologies (e.g., infection, bleeding, <u>premature rupture of membranes</u>).




### Etiology




Most cases of <u>cervical insufficiency</u> are <u>idiopathic</u>.




### <u>Risk factors</u> [[9]](/library/MwWMjn0)




* Previous midtrimester <u>pregnancy loss</u> or <u>preterm birth</u>

* Previous obstetric or gynecological trauma (e.g., <u>termination of pregnancy</u>, <u>precipitous labor</u>, <u>multiple gestations</u>, <u>conization</u>)

* Short cervical length: transvaginal cervical length < 25 mm on <u>ultrasound</u> before 24 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Cervical <u>connective tissue</u> <u>weakness</u> (e.g., <u>Ehler-Danlos syndrome</u>)

* <u>Diethylstilbestrol</u> exposure





### Clinical features




* Painless <u>cervical dilation</u> with or without prolapsed membranes

* Nonspecific findings

* <u>Pelvic</u> cramps, <u>back pain</u>

* <u>Vaginal discharge</u>: ↑ volume, yellow or blood-stained, and/or thinner consistency





### Diagnosis




* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u> in individuals with painless <u>cervical dilation</u> before 24 weeks' (may be up to 28 weeks') <u>gestation</u> or a history of second-trimester <u>preterm birth</u> or <u>pregnancy loss</u> related to painless <u>cervical dilation</u>

* A <u>short cervical length</u> is not diagnostic of <u>cervical insufficiency</u>.

* Some experts make a diagnosis of <u>cervical insufficiency</u> in patients with a <u>short cervical length</u> before 24 weeks' <u>gestation</u> in the current <u>pregnancy</u> if they have a history of ≥ 1 <u>preterm birth</u> or <u>pregnancy loss</u> related to <u>cervical dilation</u> between 16 and 36 weeks' <u>gestation</u>. [[9]](/library/MwWMjn0)[[10]](/library/wEahBm)





### Management of cervical insufficiency and short cervical length [[11]](/library/CEaqBm)




* In women with <u>risk factors</u> (e.g., previous <u>preterm birth</u>): serial cervical <u>ultrasound</u> monitoring between 16 and 24 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Intravaginal <u>progesterone</u> should be considered if the patient has a <u>short cervical length</u>.

* Cervical cerclage ;  [[10]](/library/wEahBm)[[12]](/library/9EaNBm)[[13]](/library/oeW0-40)

* Definition: placement of a supportive suture in the cervicovaginal junction to prevent <u>early pregnancy loss</u> and <u>preterm birth</u>

* Methods

* McDonald cerclage: a surgical procedure performed to prevent <u>preterm birth</u> in women with <u>cervical insufficiency</u> that involves placing a suture in the <u>cervix</u>, typically using a transvaginal approach, to reinforce cervical closure; usually removed between 36 and 37 weeks' <u>gestation</u> or at the onset of <u>preterm labor</u>.

* Shirodkar cerclage: a surgical procedure during which a suture is placed in the cervical <u>submucosal</u> tissue to treat <u>cervical insufficiency</u>; usually removed between 36 and 37 weeks' <u>gestation</u> or at the onset of <u>preterm labor</u> (can be left in place if <u>cesarean delivery</u> is planned).

* Timing: < 24 weeks' <u>gestation</u>; most commonly performed at 13–16 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Indications

* <u>Cervical dilation</u> at < 24 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* <u>Singleton pregnancy</u> with a <u>short cervical length</u> before 24 weeks' <u>gestation</u> and a history of <u>preterm birth</u> or <u>pregnancy loss</u>

* Prior <u>cerclage</u> due to <u>cervical insufficiency</u> at < 24 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Can be considered in a <u>singleton pregnancy</u> without a history of <u>preterm birth</u> if cervical length is < 10 mm before 24 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Contraindications

* <u>Preterm labor</u>

* <u>Premature rupture of membranes</u>

* <u>Chorioamnionitis</u> or vaginal infection

* ≥ 24 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* Unexplained <u>vaginal bleeding</u>

* Strict bed rest, intramuscular <u>progesterone</u> injections, and cervical pessaries are not recommended.





> [!TIP]
> A shortened cervical length is not sufficient to diagnose <u>cervical insufficiency</u>.




![Cervical cerclage](media/r3ew10humcgzv6647255esir.jpg)

## Pregnancy dermatoses

<u>Pregnancy dermatoses</u> include <u>gestational pemphigoid</u>, <u>polymorphic eruption of pregnancy</u>, and <u>intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy</u>.




### Pemphigoid gestationis [[14]](/library/FubgGv)




* Definition: <u>bullous</u>, pemphigoid-like dermatosis during <u>pregnancy</u> of unknown cause (most likely immunological)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: 1:50,000 <u>pregnancies</u> (in the US)

* Clinical features

* Commonly starts in the periumbilical region during the 2<sup>nd</sup> and <u>3<sup>rd</sup> trimester</u>

* Intensely pruritic, mostly nonblistering lesions (<u>eczema</u>, <u>urticarial</u> or <u>papular</u> lesions) on extremities and <u>mucous membranes</u>

* Grouped <u>vesicles</u> with herpetiform appearance (“gestational herpes”) usually occur as the disease advances.

* Diagnosis: The diagnosis is confirmed via <u>biopsy</u> and <u>immunofluorescence</u>.

* Treatment: <u>glucocorticoids</u> (topical or systemic) at the lowest dose needed to control disease [[15]](/library/EJd8DI0)

* Prognosis

* Usually <u>self-limited</u>; heals spontaneously after delivery, ; but associated with complications (e.g., <u>premature labor</u>, ; increased lifetime risk of autoimmune disease)

* Recurrence is possible, especially appearing:

* Spontaneously in the <u>postpartum period</u>

* In subsequent <u>pregnancies</u>

* When taking <u>contraceptives</u> containing <u>progestin</u> or <u>estrogen</u>

* During <u>menstruation</u>

* <u>Infants</u> born to women with <u>gestational pemphigoid</u> can develop transient <u>blistering</u> that resolves spontaneously.





![Manifestations of gestational pemphigoid](media/iwi1j2gy24kj8m8t4nqevic5.jpg)

Manifestations of gestational pemphigoid

![Pruritus in pregnancy](media/r45bt6jsblelyfl3p0homh5i.jpg)

Pruritus in pregnancy




### Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP)




* Description: A benign, inflammatory condition that most commonly affects <u>primiparous</u> women in the <u>third trimester</u> of <u>pregnancy</u> or immediately postpartum.

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: relatively common, occurring in ∼ 1:160 pregnant patients [[16]](/library/Ho1KW30)

* Clinical features

* Very pruritic, <u>erythematous</u> <u>papules</u> within abdominal <u>striae</u>

* Lesions can spread to the chest, back, and extremities, and coalesce into <u>urticarial</u> <u>plaques</u>, sparing the face, palms, and soles

* Lesions last 4–6 weeks and resolve spontaneously [[17]](/library/7o14W30)

* Differential diagnosis: <u>gestational pemphigoid</u>

* The early stages of PEP are similar to <u>gestational pemphigoid</u>.

* However, PEP typically begins in the <u>striae</u> (with periumbilical sparing), while the lesions in <u>gestational pemphigoid</u> are located periumbilical.

* Management: <u>topical corticosteroids</u>





![Linea nigra and polymorphic eruption of pregnancy](media/o3fm7txgvh8wduanfcxor9rn.jpg)

Linea nigra and polymorphic eruption of pregnancy

![Pruritus in pregnancy](media/r45bt6jsblelyfl3p0homh5i.jpg)

## Pregnancy luteoma

* Definition: rare, <u>benign tumors</u> that arise in response to elevated <u>hormone</u> levels (e.g., β-<u>hCG</u>) during <u>pregnancy</u>

* Clinical features

* The majority of patients are asymptomatic.

* Occasionally, they are functionally active (i.e., cause <u>androgen</u> hypersecretion) and manifest with symptoms of <u>virilization</u> of the mother or the fetus.

* Diagnostics

* <u>Pelvic</u> <u>ultrasound</u>

* Solid <u>adnexal mass</u>

* Can be unilateral or bilateral

* Significant venous or arterial flow

* 4–10 cm in diameter

* <u>Luteomas</u> are often diagnosed incidentally during <u>cesarean delivery</u>.

* Treatment

* Observation

* Most regress spontaneously postpartum.
